items.title: Dancing with Shakira at World Cup was ‘very, very, very, very, very good’ – Ghetto Kids
items.description: Ugandan dance group Ghetto Kids are celebrating another milestone after appearing at the football World Cup final half-time show on Sunday – a life-changing experience summed up by 10-year-old Sierra as “very, very, very, very, very good”. Despite critics bemoaning the addition of a Superbowl-style show to the beautiful game’s biggest event, the children’s performance alongside global stars Burna Boy and Shakira was viewed by many millions around the world. Speaking to the BBC’s Newsday programme , members of the dance troupe and their manager say that rising from humble beginnings in Uganda’s capital, Kampala, then finding fame while balancing it all with schoolwork has taken perseverance. “Never give up… pray to God. Listen to your parents, education is first, that’s all,” says Sierra. She and 11-year-old Josephine are still on a high, after their World Cup appearance midway through the game that saw Spain beat Argentina at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. “I saw Messi and Lamine Yamal!” says Josephine about the two team’s stars – Argentinian captain Lionel Messi and Spain’s teenage winger Yamal. “I was so happy to see Messi and people watching us. I felt so excited and I was smiling, and a little bit nervous,” she recalls. “Shakira, she’s very kind,” chimes in Sierra. The children gave Colombian pop star Shakira and Nigerian musician Burna Boy a big hug on stage as their performance ended – a moment their manager, Dauda Kavuma, insists was a natural show of affection, rather than clever choreography. Learning they had been picked to perform was a dream come true. The children “ran around in a circle, banging and shouting” when they learned the news, says Kavuma. “ They had already danced to Waka Waka in Britain’s Got Talent,” he explains about Shakira’s remake of the 1980s Cameroonian classic Zangaléwa by Golden Sounds . “But it was now a great moment to see that Shakira invited us… to perform with her. “It means a lot and it’s life-changing.” Kavuma’s philosophy is that there is so much talent in the ghetto, you just have to polish it. As a child he lived on the streets of Uganda’s capital before the kindness of a teacher changed his life. He wanted to give back and later became a teacher himself before creating the Ghetto Kids dance troupe – formed of homeless children and those who could not afford school fees. Frequent practice is a part of life for the Ghetto Kids, who have a huge social media following Combining a multitude of African dance styles, comedy and pure joy, they soon caught the attention of Ugandan musicians including Eddy Kenzo, who asked them to feature in some of his videos. The group’s strategy has involved harnessing the viral-making powers of the internet, and their biggest break followed in 2017 when they appeared in the music video for French Montana’s song Unforgettable – which at the time of writing has amassed more than 1.9 billion views on YouTube . That recognition opened yet more doors, leading Ghetto Kids to the final of Britain’s Got Talent in 2023, before also competing in America’s Got Talent the following year. It has also enabled Kavuma to expand his project offering housing, food and tuition to many children across Uganda. This year’s football World Cup final may have been the Ghetto Kids’ biggest stage yet, but it was not their first major sporting event. Back in 2023, the young dancers were thrilled to meet Kylian Mbappé and perform at a football half-time match in France between rivals Paris Saint-Germain and Reims. Another recent career highlight was a film being made about their story, called Ghetto Kids Documentary: No Plan B. “Education first” is the message their parents and manager have drilled into the young dancers Despite their fame, the children’s parents and manager have instilled in them an “education-first” mentality. Videos for their vast social media following are filmed at weekends, so that weekdays are largely kept free for school, Kavuma says. If they have to travel for performances, the children connect online to their teachers while away and catch up on any missed work once back in Kampala. Both Sierra and Josephine tell the BBC they plan to become doctors when they grow up but will never give up their passion for dance. “Dancing changed my life – I went to school because of dance,” says Sierra. Big hugs from Burna Boy and Shakira at the half-time show Josephine agrees: “Dance is what I know and that makes me happy because that’s my talent.” So, what do they want to say to other children who, like them, might be talented but have not had the easiest start in life? “To love themselves, believe in God, and pray. Be with their talents – don’t deny them,” answers Josephine. “And we love them.”

items.title: Medical tribunal redefines standards of ‘negligence’
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The medical tribunal has delivered two significant judgements redefining the legal standards governing professional negligence, expert medical evidence and disciplinary proceedings against registered medical practitioners. The judgements, authored by medical tribunal chairman retired justice Safdar Saleem Shahid, while deciding the connected cross appeals arising from disciplinary proceedings before the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC), articulated principles of general application extending beyond the facts of the individual dispute to formulate a comprehensive judicial framework governing professional negligence, expert evidence, procedural fairness and proportionality of disciplinary sanctions. The rulings, both available with Dawn , are expected to influence future proceedings before the PMDC, constitutional litigation and civil claims involving allegations of medical negligence. Rather than treating the appeals as a disagreement confined to one surgical procedure, the tribunal examined broader questions concerning the legal standards applicable whenever allegations of professional negligence are investigated by statutory regulatory bodies. Two rulings on appeals may influence future proceedings before PMDC, litigation and civil claims about medical negligence, misconduct In doing so, it drew on comparative common-law jurisprudence while adapting those principles to Pakistan’s statutory framework. First principle The tribunal held that medicine is not an exact science and that recognised diagnostic or surgical procedures may result in known complications despite the exercise of reasonable skill and care. Consequently, an unsuccessful treatment or adverse clinical outcome cannot, by itself, establish professional negligence. Second principle In what is regarded as an important clarification of the country’s medical law, the tribunal emphasised that professional negligence and professional misconduct cannot be treated as interchangeable expressions. Professional negligence concerns whether a doctor exercised reasonable clinical skill and judgement, whereas professional misconduct relates to breaches of ethical, statutory or professional obligations. Third principle The judgements have reaffirmed that expert medical evidence ordinarily remains indispensable in cases involving allegations of clinical negligence. However, the tribunal held that expert opinion is not conclusive merely because it originates from medical professionals. Borrowing from internationally recognised principles governing medical negligence, the tribunal observed that adjudicating authorities must independently determine whether expert opinion is logical, evidence-based and capable of withstanding objective judicial scrutiny before relying on it to impose disciplinary sanctions. Fourth principle The tribunal further ruled that disciplinary findings carrying serious professional consequences must be supported by reliable evidence and reasoned decision-making. Regulatory authorities, it observed, are required to evaluate all relevant material objectively, address the principal submissions advanced by both parties and ensure that conclusions are based upon tested evidence rather than conjecture, assumptions or unsubstantiated allegations. Fifth principle The tribunal observed that the purpose of professional discipline is to protect patients, maintain public confidence in the medical profession and uphold professional standards while ensuring fairness to practitioners. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: First phase of AJK polls begins in Mirpur division
items.description: The first phase of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) elections have begun in the 13 constituencies of Mirpur division. Polling began at 8am and will continue till 5pm. Today (Monday) has been declared a public holiday in all three districts — Bhimber, Mirpur, and Kotli — of the division to facilitate polling. A total of 288 candidates are contesting today’s election. According to the Election Commission, polling will be held at 2,316 polling stations, of which 1,241 have been declared ‘highly sensitive’ and 724 ‘sensitive’. Election monitoring has been organised through 13 zones and 205 sectors across the division, while 18,560 personnel from police and other law enforcement agencies have been deployed under a three-tier security plan. Under the arrangement, police will provide the first layer of security, Pakistan Rangers (Punjab), Pakistan Rangers (Sindh) and the Federal Constabulary the second, and the Pakistan Army the third. Around 2,100 army personnel will also be deployed, while Quick Response Force teams will remain on standby to respond to any emergency. Polls in AJK are being held in three phases over security concerns. The second and third phases are scheduled for August 2 and August 10 in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division and all 12 refugee constituencies, and 11 constituencies of Poonch division, respectively. CEC urges citizens to vote, warns against disrupting polls On Sunday, AJK Chief Election Commissioner Justice (retd) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal urged more than 1.4 million registered voters to turn out in large numbers to elect their representatives. In a video message, the CEC said elaborate security arrangements had been made for the polls, with security forces and Quick Response Force teams deployed at polling stations and security also being ensured for voters travelling to and from polling stations. He warned that anyone attempting to disrupt the polling process would face strict legal action. The warning followed the announcement by the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) on the social media about a planned long march from Mirpur division towards Muzaffarabad on Sunday. A core member of the JAAC, Umar Nazir Kashmiri, had claimed that caravans would converge at the Rawalakot sit-in, before marching towards Muzaffarabad after Zuhr prayers on the election day. However, when Mirpur DIG police was asked about the protest call given by the banned outfit, the official told Dawn on Sunday evening that not a single person had turned up anywhere to participate in any Rawalakot-bound rally. Meanwhile, AJK Chief Secretary Khushal Khan also warned of strict legal action against anyone attempting to disrupt the polling process or disturb public order afterwards. Bilawal vs Nawaz PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and ex-premier Nawaz Sharif were both participating in canvassing in the lead up to the polls, with observers seeing this election as a contest between the two. Addressing a public rally in AJK’s Mirpur on Friday as part of his party’s election campaign, Nawaz had named Bilawal and said Kashmir should not be mistaken for Kashmore, nor Mirpur for Mirpurkhas — districts of Sindh where the PPP has been in power for years. The PML-N had also given 10 e-buses to Muzaffarabad and Mirpur as a “gift” and announced development schemes, prompting the PPP to decry poll code violations. Bilawal on Sunday responded to Nawaz’s jibe, saying that whether it’s Kashmir or Kashmore, Mirpur or Mirpurkhas, their residents were “not ready to bargain away their rights”. He also directly commented on Nawaz and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s announcement of “gifting” electric buses and hospitals on wheels to people of AJK before the election. “Something built with the public’s money is not a gift from any politician — it is the public’s right,” he said, adding that he wanted to secure for the people of Kashmir the right to governance, the right to ownership, and the right to employment.

items.title: Green alternatives to oil dependence
items.description: Pakistan’s trade deficit surged to $39.47 billion in FY26, the highest in four years, highlighting the country’s deep structural dependence on imported energy. The petroleum group import bill alone reached $16.86bn, up from $15.94bn a year earlier, while crude oil imports jumped 32.1 per cent to $7.17bn. These figures underscore the urgent need to shift from imported fossil fuels to affordable green energy. Middle East conflicts and flawed energy policy have repeatedly forced Pakistan into last-minute purchases of oil and LNG at elevated spot prices. Rising shipping, insurance and geopolitical risk premiums have further inflated the country’s import bill, making energy the single largest contributor to the external imbalance. Pakistan cannot continue responding to every external shock with import contractions. The sustainable solution is to permanently reduce dependence on imported fuel by accelerating investment in solar power, battery storage and electric mobility. The government should immediately announce zero customs duty and zero sales tax for five years on solar panels, inverters, lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, e-bikes and small electric vehicles. Such a policy would lower energy costs, reduce petroleum imports, improve export competitiveness and stimulate domestic manufacturing through joint ventures and local investment. Accelerating investment in solar power, battery storage and electric mobility is a sustainable solution According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, petroleum imports reached nearly $1.91bn in June 2026, an increase of 45.5pc over June 2025. Petroleum products consistently account for 20-28pc of Pakistan’s total imports, making them the most volatile component of the trade deficit. Renewed tensions in the Middle East have again pushed Brent crude above $88 per barrel at the time of writing this article, exposing Pakistan to another round of imported inflation and external pressure. Unlike many imports, petroleum demand is difficult to reduce in the short term. Industry, transport, agriculture and electricity generation all depend heavily on imported fuels. Whenever international oil prices rise, Pakistan’s import bill immediately expands, putting pressure on foreign exchange reserves and the rupee. Pakistan, however, possesses one of the world’s highest solar irradiation levels. Yet solar adoption remains below potential because duties and taxes on inverters and batteries significantly increase installation costs. Removing these barriers would accelerate investment in utility-scale, commercial and residential solar systems while enabling reliable round-the-clock electricity through battery storage. Duty-free solar technology would directly benefit export-oriented industries such as textiles, garments, leather, sports goods and engineering products. High electricity costs remain one of the biggest disadvantages faced by Pakistani exporters compared with competitors in Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia. Affordable solar-plus-storage systems would lower production costs, improve reliability and enhance international competitiveness. Battery storage deserves equal attention. While lithium-ion batteries dominate today’s market, sodium-ion technology offers an attractive long-term alternative because sodium is cheaper, more abundant and less vulnerable to geopolitical supply disruptions. Early incentives for both technologies would help Pakistan diversify future energy storage options. Transport is another major consumer of imported petroleum. Promoting electric two- and three-wheelers through duty exemptions can significantly reduce fuel consumption, improve urban air quality and encourage local assembly and manufacturing. Combined with solar-powered charging infrastructure, electric mobility can substantially reduce oil imports while creating new employment opportunities. Lower energy costs are not only essential for reducing imports; they are equally important for increasing exports. Pakistan’s export-to-GDP ratio remains around 8-9pc, well below successful regional economies. Affordable and reliable electricity is one of the few factors the government can influence directly to improve industrial competitiveness. Over time, Pakistan can also develop a domestic green technology industry. Local assembly of solar equipment, batteries and electric vehicles can gradually evolve into manufacturing, creating skilled employment while diversifying the country’s export base beyond traditional sectors. To maximise benefits, duty exemptions should be supported by complementary reforms. Strict quality standards must prevent the import of substandard equipment. After an initial period of rapid deployment, gradually increasing local-content requirements should encourage domestic man­­­u­­­­­­acturing. The State Bank of Pakistan should expand concessional green financing to help industries and households invest in renewable energy. Net-metering and wheeling regulations should also be simplified to encourage private investment, while technical training programmes should prepare a skilled workforce for solar installation, battery maintenance and EV servicing. Although the government may initially lose some customs revenue, these losses will be outweighed by reduced petroleum imports, higher exports, increased industrial activity and lower future energy subsidies. Pakistan’s recurring balance-of-payments crises are fundamentally energy crises. Every phase of economic growth raises energy demand, increases petroleum imports, widens the trade deficit and eventually forces economic contraction. Breaking this cycle requires structural reform rather than temporary import cont­rols. Making solar panels, inverters, lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, e-bikes and electric vehicles duty-free offers one of the highest-return policy interventions available today. It would permanently reduce the country’s largest import category, lower production costs for exporters and lay the foundation for a modern green manufacturing industry. The $39.47bn trade deficit cannot be eliminated through a single policy measure. However, reducing dependence on imp­orted energy is perhaps the most effective long-term strategy available. Pakistan has abundant sunshine, a large domestic market and growing energy demand. With clear policies and timely implementation, green technology can transform these advantages into stronger exports, lower imp­orts and sustainable economic growth. The writer is a former Vice President of KCCI and an international trade expert. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Under the shadow of melting monoliths
items.description: IN THE picturesque valley of Golen, located over 20km northeast of Chitral city, summer once unfolded in all its resplendence. Visitors from across the district would flock to Golen during the warmer months to enjoy its cool mountain air, try their hand at trout fishing, and marvel at its lush green meadows. Yet, in recent years, that once-bountiful summer has become a source of anxiety for Golen natives. The cause lies in the glaciers, those primordial agglomerations of ice that had stood sentinel over the valley for centuries, which are now melting at an alarming rate and forming large, unstable lakes in their wake. On the evening of July 7, 2019, one such glacial lake burst its banks and ravaged the valley, destroying homes and orchards, damaging the headworks of the 108MW Golen Gol hydropower project, plunging the district into darkness for several days. The very next year, Golen experienced another glacial lake outburst flood (Glof). With over 80 potentially dangerous glacial lakes dotting the region, communities in the Hindu Kush live in fear of advancing, unfrozen glaciers Last week, as rain fell over the valley, the villagers endured a sleepless night. Safia Bibi, a resident of Golen, told Dawn that terror gripped them when the rain began. “Initially we were terrified,” she recounted, “but later, when the men told us it was too cold and that we should not fear a flood from these clouds, only then did our frayed nerves calm.” Safia remembers all too well what happened in 2020, when she had to make a dash for safety, clutching her one-year-old daughter in the pouring rain as a Glof carrying huge boulders and debris descended on her village. A portion of her under-construction home was badly damaged, and a few months later, her husband purchased land in a neighbouring village to relocate, due to constant threat of Glofs in their native area. But Golen is not unique, and other remote valleys across the Hindu Kush are grappling with the same dilemma. Their communities, long ensconced in geographical remoteness, lived in harmony with nature for centuries. Now, extreme weather has thrust them onto the front lines of an unfolding climate catastrophe — one in whose making they have played no role and to which they have contributed nothing. As climate change wreaks havoc across the globe, unleashing unprecedented consequences on even the planet’s most pristine and remote corners, its impact is especially pronounced in the Hindu Kush, where communities have long lived in close proximity to rugged, unforgiving terrain. Over 130 ‘potentially dangerous’ lakes Figures released by the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco) on its ‘SpaceforClimate’ portal paint a worrying picture for millions living across the Hindu Kush. The agency’s June 5 update recorded 24 unfrozen glacial lakes in northern Pakistan, with 15 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — 10 of them in Upper and Lower Chitral, three in Swat, and one in Lower Dir. By July 2, that number had nearly doubled to 40, with Suparco noting that most lakes were concentrated in Chitral, Upper Dir and Swat. The agency said it is regularly monitoring Potentially Dangerous Glacial Lakes (PDGLs) via satellite imagery to support early warning and preparedness for Glof hazards, drawing on a combined list of 131 PDGL locations supplied by the Provincial Disaster Management Authorities (PDMAs) of KP and Gilgit-Baltistan and Wapda’s Glacier Monitoring and Research Centre. “As expected with rising summer temperatures, the number of unfrozen glacial lakes is increasing… indicating accelerated seasonal melting,” Suparco said, adding that most unfrozen lakes remain within their previously recorded maximum extents. A lake becomes a greater concern, it noted, when its water extent exceeds historical highs, since this can signal increased storage and higher risk of moraine dam instability. The agency urged authorities to maintain heightened preparedness in downstream valleys given the continuing temperature rise. Separately, data from KP’s Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) shows 63 Glof-vulnerable lakes and 21 potentially dangerous ones spread across five districts: nine vulnerable sites in Chitral (Upper and Lower), 18 in Upper Dir, 31 in Swat, and five in Upper Kohistan. All 21 potentially dangerous lakes are confined to Upper and Lower Chitral. ‘Especially vulnerable’ Chitral-based glacier researcher Hamid Ahmed Mir, who has visited many of these sites, told Dawn that the region’s glaciers are unusually vulnerable because of their small size. With the exception of Tirich-Concordia and Chiantar — the latter feeding the Kabul River — nearly all Hindu Kush glaciers are small, making them highly sensitive to temperature spikes. These ‘water towers’ are likely to assume even greater importance over the coming years as the water war between India and Pakistan intensifies. He also pointed to steep slope gradients and high seismic activity, noting five to six fault lines run beneath Chitral alone, alongside a high frequency of minor earthquakes. Much of the region’s development has been unplanned, often ignoring its fragile ecosystem and lacking proper risk assessments or environmental impact studies. For example, he cited the use of explosives to dig the three-kilometre headrace tunnel for the Golen Gol hydropower project, inaugurated in 2018 — two years before a major Glof struck the valley. Mir also pointed to Chitral’s status as an air-shed valley, where surrounding high mountains trap air, dust and pollutants. His recent research on dust generation from traffic on the largely unpaved, poorly maintained, and decade-long-under-construction Chitral–Mastuj road found that the 110-kilometre stretch could be producing approximately 40,000 tonnes of airborne or fugitive dust every year, including nearly 9,600 tonnes of respirable PM₁₀ particulate matter. “The Chitral–Mastuj road is a vital transportation corridor that supports communities, trade, and tourism. However, its predominantly unpaved surface also represents a significant source of fugitive dust,” the research paper noted, adding that preliminary engineering estimates suggest around 28,000 tonnes of that dust settles within the surrounding valley annually. The paper warned the implications extend far beyond roadside nuisance, as dust affects human health, agriculture, alpine ecosystems, water resources, and glacier stability — potentially amplifying the impacts of climate change in one of Pakistan’s most environmentally sensitive mountain regions. It recommended improved road surfacing, dust suppression, vegetation restoration, and systematic environmental monitoring to protect both local air quality and long-term water security in Chitral and further downstream. Government response KP PDMA Director General Arifullah Awan told Dawn the provincial government was pursuing both mitigation and adaptation strategies to secure the region against climatic threats. At least 85 early warning systems, rain gauges and other sensors have been installed across Lower and Upper Chitral, Upper Dir, Swat and Upper Kohistan with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). In addition, community-based disaster risk management committees — including union council secretaries and local members — have been formed, with alert times ranging from 20 to 35 minutes. To protect the early warning systems from vandalism, district- and tehsil-level committees have also been set up, with FIRs lodged in the past over damage to the equipment. The government is also pursuing afforestation, environment-friendly infrastructure, and climate-resilient construction as part of its broader mitigation and adaptation strategy, Awan added. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Samsung Elec wins $200 billion Broadcom AI chip partnership, boosting foundry push
items.description: Samsung Electronics said on Saturday it struck a pact with U.S. chip designer Broadcom to widen cooperation across memory chips, contract ​chip making and advanced packaging envisaged to exceed $200 billion until ‌2030. Winning long-term production commitments from Broadcom, one of the world’s leading custom AI chip designers, could boost utilisation at Samsung’s advanced manufacturing facilities to pull ahead in the ​race to supply AI chips. “The expanded collaboration … reflects Samsung’s focus on ​supporting customers with end-to-end semiconductor technologies across an increasingly diverse range ⁠of AI and high-performance computing applications,” the company said in a ​statement. The tie-up comes as global technology companies increasingly develop their own custom AI ​accelerators, rather than relying solely on general-purpose graphics processors, driving demand for specialised chip design and manufacturing partnerships. The two firms’ memorandum of understanding underscores Samsung’s efforts to beef up ​its position in AI semiconductors by expanding its long-term ties with Broadcom ​amid growing demand up for custom AI processors. The next five years of collaboration will ‌combine ⁠Broadcom’s expertise in designing application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), or chips for specific tasks, with Samsung’s manufacturing capabilities. The deal provides for Broadcom’s next-generation communications chips, designed for high-speed data transfer, to be made with Samsung’s sub-2-nanometre process technology, Samsung said. The two ​will also collaborate ​on next-generation high-bandwidth ⁠memory (HBM) products. The partnership could help strengthen Samsung’s foundry business, as it seeks to narrow the gap with industry leader ​TSMC (2330.TW), opens new tab by wooing major technology customers. Last month, co-CEO and ​chip division ⁠head Jun Young-hyun said he discussed next-generation foundry cooperation with Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, including future HBM4E and HBM5 memory products. Samsung said this year it ⁠expected ​to secure more advanced 2-nanometre foundry orders in ​the near term after discussions with major tech companies. Last year, it won a $16.5-billion contract to ​make logic chips for EV maker Tesla .

items.title: India’s Gen Z dents Modi’s aura ahead of state polls
items.description: A CHILD holds a placard during a gathering in solidarity with the Cockroach Janta Party in Mumbai.—AFP • Indian PM posts video promising remedial steps amid growing youth anger • Experts say social media-driven activism signals changing political trends NEW DELHI: Nearly five weeks after the leaders of India’s youth Cockr­oach Janta Party (CJP) began their protest dema­n­ding the resignation of the education minister over exam paper leaks, Pri­me Minister Narendra Modi, 75, posted a rare selfie video: he said he was pained by their suffering and promised remedial steps The video, posted late on Thursday on Instagram, where CJP amassed 22 million mainly Gen Z followers in a matter of days in May, was not enough to satisfy the thousands of protesters who had gathered in central Delhi, braved a massive police crackdown days earlier, and then inspired protests across the country. On Saturday, the education minister stepped down , meeting the protesters’ main demand, in a rare such setback for Modi. The resignation of Educ­ation Minister Dharm­endra Pradhan hands a clear win to the CJP, whose young supporters have openly mocked Modi through raps, placards and graffiti, an almost unthinkable development only weeks earlier in a country whose politics has been almost fully dominated by Modi since he came to power in 2014. “A large number of people who were at the protest may actually be his supporters and that’s quite different from other kinds of protests in the past,” said Sanjay Srivastava, anthropology professor at SOAS University of London. “What might be interpreted as a win is the fact that there is now a much wider cross-section of people questioning the government. A much wider cross-section has begun to question the idea that the ruling party is necessarily good for the country.” The protests were triggered by a leaked medical-entrance exam, but there are other issues, mainly youth unemployment and fear among the young that AI could take their jobs in places such as IT back offices that India is known for, analysts said. “The paper leak is a trigger point,” political analyst Amitabh Tiwari said. “It is largely a reflection of the anxiety, nervousness, discontent, frustration and anger among the youth.” Modi’s senior ministerial colleague Rajnath Singh said the government’s “top priority remains to understand our students’ genuine concerns, address them promptly, and ensure that they know their voices are being heard”. Govt out of touch with what Gen Z wants Indians aged 18 to 40 are estimated to make up abo­ut 40 per cent of the population but hold only about 10pc of seats in the lower house of parliament, down from more than double that in the 1950s, Tiwari said. The cabinet’s average age is more than 60. Tho­u­gh the CJP is not a political party, all opposition parties have tried to cash in on the rare opening they have seen in the protests against Modi, by taking up the cause of the students. The first tests of the youth anger could be in elections next year in the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, in Punjab and Modi’s home state of Gujarat. The BJP runs both Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat. The bigger risk for Modi could lie in the 2029 national election if the CJP turns itself into a party. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has said no decision had been made so far on joining electoral politics. Some analysts say young voters have hitherto largely cast ballots along religious or caste lines, benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. But things may be changing. An actor — running for his own party and allied with opposition parties — was recently elected chief minister in the prosperous southern state of Tamil Nadu, propelled by his Instagram-first Gen Z fanbase. “This has been a moment of reckoning for PM Modi — and it shows how they are completely out of touch with what Gen Z wants,” said author Anurag Minus Verma. “For years, the BJP’s digital political strategy was centred on platforms like X, where much of the political conversation took place. But that conversation has increasingly shif­ted to Instagram now, particularly among younger users.” The BJP may rule most of India, and calls itself the world’s largest political party, but it has managed just 10 million Instagram followers in years, less than half what the CJP gained in days. The BJP has 23 million followers on X and 18 million on Facebook, though Mo­di’s personal followers on all three social media platforms are massive, ranging between 60 and 107 million. India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi annou­nced Sunday a special task force to reform the country’s exam system, a day after his administration’s education minister resigned. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Shifting geopolitics of tech
items.description: The development and governance of artificial intelligence should be a global effort. It should not be a solo performance by any single country, but rather “a symphony of global cooperation”, Chinese President Xi Jinping said at the opening of the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 17. The remark encapsulated the broader message that extended well beyond technology. It was as much about geopolitics and emerging contests for global influence as about AI. For Pakistan, the conference deserved far greater attention than it received. The country is among the 29 founding members of the newly established World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), a China-led intergovernmental initiative formally launched on July 16. Yet its creation and the opportunities it presents for Pakistan and other developing economies received little discussion in the country’s mainstream media. Waico has the potential to become an important platform for countries seeking to participate more actively in the AI revolution rather than remaining dependent on technologies developed and controlled elsewhere. For Pakistan, where fiscal constraints, limited computing infrastructure and shortages of skilled professionals continue to impede digital transformation, collaboration on AI research, training and infrastructure could prove especially valuable. China’s push for a more inclusive global AI order offers us opportunities The Shanghai conference underscored a broader reality: artificial intelligence is no longer merely a technological issue but a central element of global strategic competition. China is increasingly positioning itself as an alternative to the United States in shaping AI governance. Its message is that access to AI models, computing resources, expertise and infrastructure should not be restricted to a handful of advanced economies but should also be available to developing countries at an affordable cost. Waico reflects this vision. Its founding members include several major Global South countries, among them Indonesia, Brazil, Malaysia, South Africa, Senegal, Russia and Pakistan. Officially, the organisation aims to promote international collaboration on AI while encouraging regulatory frameworks that ensure the technology remains safe and beneficial. At the same time, it provides Beijing with a platform to strengthen its influence over emerging international AI governance, particularly as global rules are still taking shape. This initiative unfolds against the backdrop of an intensifying US-China technology rivalry. Washington has imposed restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductor technologies on national security grounds, while Beijing has responded by limiting exports of critical minerals and other dual-use technologies. Increasingly, competition extends beyond hardware to encompass AI standards, supply chains and the rules governing the technology’s global development and use. Although US export controls continue to limit China’s access to the most advanced chips, Beijing retains significant strengths. It has invested heavily in computing infrastructure and data centres, dominates the production of several rare earth minerals essential to advanced technologies, and possesses substantial electricity-generation capacity to support energy-intensive AI systems. China is also distinguishing itself through international technology partnerships. At the Shanghai conference, it pledged 5,000 AI training and seminar opportunities for developing countries, announced plans for regional AI cooperation centres, and offered support for deploying Chinese AI models and applications overseas. For countries such as Pakistan, these initiatives address a pressing challenge. Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming a general-purpose technology with applications across education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, finance, defence and public administration. Nations that fail to develop domestic computing capacity, technical expertise and supporting infrastructure risk becoming long-term consumers of foreign AI systems rather than active participants in their development. This concern featured prominently throughout the Shanghai conference. Participants argued that international AI governance should encourage wider participation rather than create regulatory barriers that entrench existing technological advantages. United Nations Technology Envoy Amandeep Singh Gill similarly stressed the importance of ensuring that AI capabilities do not remain concentrated within a small number of countries and regions. China has sought to position itself as a partner in addressing this imbalance. Xi pledged support for developing countries in strengthening AI innovation, applications and governance. The appeal of this approach lies not only in access to technology but also in the accompanying investment in skills and institutional capacity. Nevertheless, strategic considerations are inseparable from these initiatives. China’s outreach coincides with parallel US efforts to build international technology partnerships and secure AI-related supply chains. Waico therefore represents more than a technical cooperation mechanism; it also forms part of a broader contest between competing visions of technological leadership. Pakistan’s National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025 aligns with many of the priorities highlighted through Waico, particularly in expanding AI infrastructure, mobilising investment and strengthening human capital. Likewise, the AI Seekho programme’s objective of training one million people could provide a stronger foundation for meaningful participation in the global AI economy if implemented effectively. Realising these opportunities, however, will require more than policy commitments. Islamabad must identify practical areas of cooperation with China and other Waico members, including research partnerships, workforce development, computing infrastructure and technology transfer. Equally important, it should use its membership to advocate for international AI governance frameworks that reflect the needs and developmental realities of emerging economies rather than reinforcing existing technological inequalities. The global AI race is well underway. For Pakistan and other developing countries, the promise of “AI for all” will ultimately depend not on access alone but on their ability to build, adapt and govern artificial intelligence as active participants in its future. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Still unprepared
items.description: EVEN as Pakistan counts around 100 deaths since the onset of the monsoon season on June 26, it is bracing for another spell of heavy rain. The Met Office has forecast widespread rain and thunderstorms through July 28, while the NDMA has warned of rising river levels, flash floods, urban flooding and landslides across large parts of the country. From Gilgit-Baltistan, where glacial lake outburst floods have severed roads, left tourists stranded and disrupted electricity to Punjab’s inundated cities and swelling rivers, Pakistan is confronting a nationwide emergency rather than a handful of isolated weather events. Lahore has recorded its heaviest rainfall of the season so far, Gujranwala and Sialkot have witnessed extensive flooding, while roads, homes, crops, livestock and public infrastructure have suffered much damage. We are reminded once more of how quickly a weather emergency can become a humanitarian one. The lesson of the devastating 2022 floods was that climate adaptation must become a permanent function of government. Four years later, many of the same weaknesses persist. Every monsoon exposes clogged drains, encroachments on waterways, fragile buildings, poorly maintained roads, fragmented institutions and delayed relief. Official claims of improved drainage and successful desilting deserve recognition where they have demonstrably reduced waterlogging, but they also warrant scrutiny when major roads remain submerged, sinkholes appear after heavy rain, communities are cut off for days and residents are left to empty flooded homes with buckets. Climate change is undoubtedly intensifying extreme weather, yet governance failures continue to magnify its human cost. Adaptation cannot consist of emergency meetings and relief announcements alone; it must be reflected in resilient infrastructure, stronger planning and accountable institutions. With more rain forecast, the priority must be to prevent further loss of life. Rescue teams, boats, food, medicines, generators and communications equipment should be pre-positioned in vulnerable districts, while warnings must reach communities in local languages through every available medium. Roads to isolated northern valleys should be restored urgently, with helicopters deployed wherever ground access remains impossible. Power distribution companies must secure hazardous installations, and administrations should close dangerous underpasses, riverbanks and mountain routes before tragedies occur. Beyond the present emergency, governments should publish district-level flood-risk maps, enforce bans on construction over drains and floodplains, expand glacial monitoring and early-warning systems, and subject preparedness claims to independent audits. Pakistan cannot prevent the monsoon, but it can stop treating predictable hazards as annual surprises. After all, preparedness is judged not by official briefings, but by lives protected. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Residents cash in on Dubai real estate cooldown
items.description: DUBAI: Just over a year after moving to Dubai, Steve found himself moving unexpectedly up the property ladder, taking advantage of a cooling real estate market amid the Middle East war. His new apartment is larger and closer to work than his previous resident, but the rent is nonetheless 15 per cent cheaper, he said, using a pseudonym due to Dubai’s sensitivity on the matter. When he arrived in Dubai last year, “it was really difficult to get a place in this area and the rents had gone up by a lot”, said the 35-year-old, who works in the media sector. Dubai’s property market — a pillar of its economy — has soared in recent years, buoyed by the arrival of international high-net-worth individuals attracted by the glamorous lifestyle on offer in the emirate. Agent says there are people who think this is the right time to invest, amid Mideast conflict But the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February has dampened growth, as targets in Dubai came under fire in the early days of Iran’s retaliation against American allies in the region. Even some of its most iconic sites, such as Burj Al-Arab and the Palm Jumeirah, were considered safe, dealing a blow to the city whose population is more than 90pc foreigners. Hostilities resumed in July, following an April ceasefire , but Dubai has so far not been in the firing line. But its image as a city that is “safe no matter what” has yet to recover from the blow it was dealt, said a real estate agent, speaking on condition of anonymity. ‘Grey area’ Today, she said, “we are in some sort of grey area. I’m getting a split sentiment; people think this has destabilised the region for a long time… And there are people who say this is the right time to invest.” Clients have not completely disappeared, the agent said, but the margins for negotiation have expanded. “Since the war, the market has shifted from a seller’s market to a buyer’s market,” she claimed. British real estate consultancy Knight Frank said, “We have already noted prices ebbing widely across the city’s mainstream market by between 5pc and 20pc, depending on location”, after having surged by an average of 82.9pc since 2021. Property giant Emaar nonetheless announced last month a massive $55 billion project in the heart of Dubai, hoping to attract some 150,000 residents, signalling its confidence in the market’s ability to bounce back. Binghatti, another major developer, said it had sold two luxury apartments in the centre in June, at $54 million and $19m, respectively. According to a report by the Betterhomes agency, based on official figures, sales transaction values fell in the second quarter of 2026 by 45pc year on year, with the luxury sector hit particularly hard. But chief executive Richard Waind nonetheless insisted that the situation has improved over the past weeks. “We’re starting to see demand increase again through June and then into this month, both in terms of buyer activity and buyer deals happening,” he said. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Frasers weighs Hugo Boss CEO role for Murray, The Times reports

In June, Frasers launched ​an all-cash takeover offer for Hugo ​Boss at €38 per share, or about €2 billion ($2.28 billion), an ‌offer ⁠the German group urged its shareholders to reject , saying it was “financially inadequate”. Frasers said last week its offer remained open, with the initial ​acceptance period ​running until ⁠July 27. Founded in 1924, Hugo Boss is Germany’s largest premium ​fashion house with annual revenue topping €4.3 ​billion ⁠in 2025. Reuters could not immediately verify The Times report. items.title: Gabon opposition leader jailed for political reasons, his lawyers say
items.description: Gabon’s main opposition leader, Alain Claude Bilie By Nze, has been in jail for more than three months after the ​government resurrected an 18-year-old private financial dispute as a pretext ‌to sideline him, his lawyers said in a statement. Nze was serving as prime minister when Brice Oligui Nguema, Gabon’s current president, took power in a coup in ​2023, and he unsuccessfully challenged Nguema in an election last ​year. Nze’s party, “Together for Gabon”, reported on Nze’s imprisonment on its ⁠Facebook page. Nze’s lawyers said in a statement that he has spent ​100 days in “political and arbitrary” solitary confinement after being arrested on ​April 15. The basis for his arrest was a private dispute over about 7,600 euros ($8,650) dating to 2008, they said. His party said he was accused of fraud ​and breach of trust in that dispute. Nze has been confined to ​a five-square-metre cell without light at a prison in the capital, Libreville, his ‌lawyers ⁠said. His lawyers said that they have not been allowed to inspect case files and that the investigating judge has said he no longer has those documents. A Libreville appeals court rejected a defence request to annul ​proceedings on June ​2. Gabon’s Justice Ministry did ⁠not respond to a request for comment. “A man is being held on the basis of a case ​file his defence has never been permitted to see,” ​Nze’s counsel, ⁠Arthur Vercken, said in the statement. The August 2023 coup in Gabon ended the more than five-decade rule of Ali Bongo and his family . Nguema ⁠was elected president in ​a vote intended to return the oil-producing ​Central African country to civilian rule.

Ve édition du Salon de la mangue: la transformation locale au cœur de la souveraineté agro-industrielle
items.description: La Ve édition du Salon de la mangue (SAMA) s’est tenue les 24 et 25 juillet 2026 à Bobo-Dioulasso. Placée sur le thème : « Vers une souveraineté agro-industrielle : bâtir une filière mangue compétitive par la transformation, la logistique et le financement », cette édition tenue en deux jours ambitionne de faire de la filière mangue un véritable moteur de création de valeur, d’emplois et de souveraineté économique au Burkina Faso. Bobo-Dioulasso, principal bassin de production de mangues du Burkina Faso, a accueilli la Ve édition du Salon de la mangue (SAMA) les 24 et 25 juillet 2026. Organisé par la Chambre de commerce et d’industrie du Burkina Faso (CCI-BF), en collaboration avec l’Association pour la promotion de la mangue du Burkina (APROMAB) et la Grappe mangue de Bobo-Dioulasso (GRAMABO), l’évènement a réuni producteurs, transformateurs, exportateurs, chercheurs, partenaires techniques et financiers autour d’une même ambition : accélérer la modernisation et la compétitivité de cette filière stratégique. Dans le message d’ouverture des travaux, le vendredi 24 juillet 2026, le gouverneur de la région du Guiriko, Mariama Konaté, a réaffirmé au nom des ministres en charge du commerce et de l’agriculture la volonté du gouvernement d’accompagner la transformation structurelle de la filière. Avec une production annuelle estimée à 360 000 tonnes, la mangue s’impose comme l’une des principales spéculations fruitières du Burkina Faso. La filière, a laissé entendre le gouverneur Konaté, génère chaque année entre 15 et 17 milliards de francs CFA de recettes d’exportation et procure près de 63 800 emplois directs. Le Burkina Faso, a-t-elle poursuivi, est également le premier exportateur africain de mangue séchée, une performance qui traduit les efforts consentis par les différents maillons de la chaîne de valeurs. « Toutefois, les performances enregistrées ne doivent pas masquer les difficultés persistantes. Le faible taux de transformation locale, estimé à environ 30%, les pertes post-récolte dues aux mouches des fruits, le coût élevé de l’énergie, les insuffisances logistiques ainsi que l’accès limité aux technologies modernes et aux financements demeurent les principaux freins au développement du secteur », a indexé Mariama Konaté. Pour y faire face, le gouvernement, a-t-elle dit, entend renforcer les investissements dans l’industrialisation, l’innovation, la qualité des produits et la conquête de nouveaux marchés. Le président de la Chambre de commerce et d’industrie du Burkina Faso, Achille Sow, a rappelé que le SAMA est devenu un espace stratégique de concertation et de promotion économique. Mobiliser tous les acteurs autour de la chaîne de valeurs Selon lui, la filière fait vivre des milliers de producteurs, de transformateurs, de commerçants, de transporteurs et d’exportateurs, tout en offrant des opportunités d’emplois aux jeunes et aux femmes. Pour lui, les panels, expositions et rencontres d’affaires prévus durant le salon devront déboucher sur des partenariats solides et des solutions concrètes pour lever les contraintes qui pèsent sur la filière. Dans la même dynamique, le parrain de cette édition, Idrissa Nassa, par la voix de son représentant, El hadj Boubacar Barro, par ailleurs président du Conseil régional du patronat du Guiriko (CRPB), a appelé à une mobilisation générale autour de trois priorités : développer les capacités nationales de transformation, améliorer les infrastructures logistiques et faciliter l’accès aux financements. A ses yeux, la souveraineté agro-industrielle passe nécessairement par une plus grande valorisation locale de la production et par des investissements soutenus dans les unités de transformation. Il a également invité les investisseurs nationaux et étrangers à saisir les opportunités qu’offre la filière mangue. Pour le directeur général de la CCI-BF, Seydou Tou, le salon constitue avant tout un cadre de réflexion destiné à identifier des solutions durables aux difficultés de la filière. Il a insisté sur la nécessité de renforcer la concertation entre les différents acteurs afin de préserver la contribution du secteur à l’économie nationale. Même son de cloche chez les professionnels. Le président de l’Association professionnelle de la mangue du Burkina (APROMAB), Yaya Koné, a salué l’accompagnement de l’Etat tout en relevant les conséquences de la crise énergétique qui a contraint près d’une centaine d’unités de transformation à ralentir ou suspendre leurs activités cette année. Il a également évoqué les dégâts causés par les mouches des fruits, avant de réaffirmer la détermination des acteurs à maintenir le Burkina Faso au premier rang africain de la mangue séchée et à accroître les exportations vers les marchés internationaux. Kamélé FAYAMA

items.title: Japanese monk asks Buddhists to visit Taxila for peace prayers
items.description: TAXILA: A 76-year-old Japanese Buddhist monk has appealed to monks and followers of Buddhism across the world to gather at Pakistan’s ancient Dharmarajika Stupa in Taxila for a collective prayer for global peace, saying the teachings of the Buddha that once spread from the historic centre of Gandhara should again inspire humanity at a time of growing global conflict. Speaking to journalists after offering prayers for peace at the nearly 2,000-year-old Dharmarajika Stupa, Japanese monk Junsei Terasawa said the world was passing through a period marked by conflicts, violence and human suffering, making the Buddha’s timeless message of compassion, non-violence and reconciliation more relevant than ever. “The message of peace was raised from Taxila and flourished across the globe, and today, when the world is once again facing conflict and uncertainty, that message must rise again from this sacred land,” Monk Terasawa expressed. Japanese Buddhist monk Junsei Terasawa San celebrated the enduring legacy of peace, harmony, and interfaith understanding on a month-long pilgrimage across Pakistan, visiting some of the country’s most significant Buddhist heritage sites. His spiritual journey has taken him to ancient stupas and monastic complexes in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, including the renowned archaeological remains in the Swat Valley, where he offered prayers and reflected on the enduring legacy of the Buddha’s teachings. For decades, Terasawa has been globally recognised for his dedication to peace-building through non-violent action and interfaith dialogue. His humanitarian mission has taken him to regions affected by armed conflict across Eurasia, where he has organised peace marches, led prayer gatherings and supported initiatives aimed at promoting reconciliation and human dignity. During periods of conflict in Iraq, Chechnya and, more recently, Ukraine, he continued advocating peaceful coexistence through spiritual outreach and public prayer. His work has focused on fostering understanding among people of different cultures and faiths, encouraging dialogue instead of confrontation, supporting the preservation of Buddhist cultural heritage, and advocating for a world free from the threat of nuclear weapons. Throughout his journeys, he has consistently emphasised that lasting peace begins with respect for the shared humanity of all people, regardless of nationality or religion. Standing at the revered Buddhist monument, where archaeologists discovered sacred relics traditionally associated with the Buddha during excavations, Terasawa described Dharmarajika as one of the most spiritually significant sites in the Buddhist world and an enduring symbol of peace. Japanese Buddhist monk Junsei Terasawa underscored the enduring historical and spiritual ties between the ancient Buddhist civilisation of Gandhara and Japan, describing the region as one of the principal sources of the religious and philosophical traditions that later shaped Japanese society. The monk also praised the artistic achievements of the Gandhara civilisation, saying its distinctive Buddhist sculptures and iconography, developed through a fusion of regional and classical influences, left a lasting impression on Buddhist art across East Asia. He observed that many of the visual representations of the Buddha found in Japan reflect artistic concepts that can be traced back to the ancient workshops of Gandhara. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Lull in Iran, US fighting ‘achieved by fresh round of diplomacy’
items.description: • Diplomatic sources say Pakistan remained in touch with Tehran, Washington, Riyadh and Beijing during latest US bombing campaign • Turkish FM reaches out to Qatari, Pakistani leadership • Waltz says lull in strikes is Trump ‘making room for talks’ • Iran also stops retaliatory attacks on US bases • US media claims ammunition shortages, generals’ opposition forced president to halt bombing WASHINGTON / TEHRAN: As US hostilities towards Iran ease, diplomatic sources in Washington said that Pakistan and other mediators had played a significant role in efforts that helped halt the second round of bombing and create conditions for another pause in fighting. After 13 nights of intensifying US airstrikes on Iran, the Pentagon abruptly suspended the campaign late on Friday, with no attacks reported on either Saturday or Sunday. Iran, which had been following each night of US attacks with its own strikes on neighbouring cou­n­­­tries that host American bases, has also so far held fire for two days. Diplomatic sources in the US capital said Pakistan had maintained communication with Tehran, Washington, Riyadh and Beijing during the US bombing campaign, arguing that these channels helped preserve space for diplomacy at a time of heightened tensions. Islamabad continued diplomatic outreach at multiple levels, they said, including contacts between senior officials, engagement with diplomatic counterparts and discussions with policymakers in Washington. They maintained that Pakis­tan’s position remained that dialogue was the only sustainable path toward ending the confrontation. The diplomatic push continued over the weekend, with Turkish media reporting contacts betw­een Foreign Minister Hakan Fid­an and a host of regional leaders, including Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir. According to the Anadolu news agenc­y, Fidan discussed the negotiation process between Teh­ran and Washington with Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammed bin Abdul­rahman Al Thani and Pakistan’s army chief. Fidan held separate calls with PM Al Thani and FM Munir, the news agency quoted Turkish diplomatic sources as saying. According to Anadolu, Islamabad and Doha have intensified the exchange of messages between the warring sides after Washington and Tehran communicated their responses to a joint formula to end the months-long war. Depleting ammo? The diplomatic push was confirmed by the US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told Fox News on Sunday that Trump had decided to pause attacks to allow more time for diplomacy. While forces remained “locked and loaded”, he said Trump was “giving talks some space… a little bit of room”. American media reported that Trump called off his campaign of strikes after being advised by top military and civilian aides against further escalating the war he launched alongside Israel in February. CNN and the New York Times said Pentagon Chief of Staff Dan Caine had pointed to the depletion of stocks of Patriot air defence missiles, which US forces have relied on to defend bases in the Middle East. CNN reported Vice President JD Vance had also expressed reservations. Plans to escalate the campaign have been shelved in part because of those shrinking supplies, according to NYT . Trump also faces the risk of a wider Middle East war, the estrangement of vulnerable Gulf allies and further shocks to the global economy, the newspaper said. Meanwhile, Axios reported that the overall commander of US forces in the Middle East, Admiral Brad Cooper, had advised halting the US bombing campaign because it had reached the limits of its effectiveness. Prior to Friday, the US military had carried out strikes on Iran for 13 consecutive nights, in the largest rekindling of the almost five-month-old war since an April ceasefire. But two consecutive nights have now passed without bombing. “These attacks continued until two nights ago, but over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks,” said Iran’s army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia. “Since… our strategy has essentially been retaliatory, we have also halted our retaliatory operations.” Unconfirmed Iranian media reports on Sunday said an oil tanker had been damaged by a sea mine. With input from Monitoring Desk and Agencies Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: President, PM, others return gifts to Toshakhana
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Presi­dent Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and other federal cabinet members received dozens of gifts from foreign dignitaries this year, with the items being deposited in Toshakhana. The information ministry recently issued details of gifts received by the premier, deputy premier and other officials over the past three months, as the cabinet division also made available on its official website records of gifts received by officeholders since 2002 although the names of foreign dignitaries who presented the gifts were not disclosed. Following the release of the latest Toshakhana rec­o­rds, Information Mini­ster Attaullah Tarar told Dawn that the government periodically publishes details of gifts received by officials and that the latest information covered the previous three months. Interestingly, the cabinet division’s website, while releasing details of gifts, mentioned that the evaluation [of these gifts] was under process. A disclaimer issued by the cabinet division said, “This data/list is provided on federal government dir­ections as per the rec­ord available and is based on the information/gifts decl­a­red or deposited by the persons and departments responsible for it under the policy prevalent at that time. The cabinet division is not responsible for any error or omissions made by those individuals/departments.” Tarar said the government regularly uploads details of deposited gifts and that the complete information was available on the portal. “We upload [details of gifts] periodically. All deposited gifts are uploaded, and the whole information is on the portal,” he said, adding that the published records included gifts received by the president, prime minister, deputy prime minister, ministers and government officers. “The only information we do not reveal is the name of the dignitary who has gifted,” he remarked. According to these records, President Zardari received a tea set and a sword on Jan 2. The president’s other gifts included a golden desert model, a woollen overcoat, a Vacheron Constantin Geneve wristwatch, a decoration piece, a ceremonial sabre set, a chessboard, a decorative serving bowl and an oil painting. First lady Assefa Bhutto-Zardari and her sister, Bakhtawar Bhutto-Zardari, each received a necklace on Jan 20 and a jewellery set on Feb 10. The first lady also received a Kumis set. PM Shehbaz received a shield and a souvenir on Jan 5, as well as a portrait, multiple shields, a tie, frames, swords, and a box containing a necklace, a ring and an earring. Other gifts include a Rolex watch bearing the numbers 55370 and model 126300 and serial number M8R25782; a second Rolex watch with the number 53286; a coin; a traditional dress; a box containing a Patek Philippe watch with the model number 7808546; a clock model; a sugar bowl; a car model; and various cups, models, pens and cufflinks. Deputy PM Dar received a decoration piece and a traditional Chinese stamp on Jan 12. His other gifts included a Burmese string puppet, a traditional Myanmar culture frame, a Rolex watch with the model number 9G16J077, a vase, a medal, a Chinese leather belt, an Egyptian statue, a pen and a cufflink set. Federal Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Khan Cheema received a book titled “Uzbekistan” and a T-shirt on Jan 12, while Economic Affairs Secretary M. Humair Karim received a superior ballpoint pen the same day. Tarar received a Rolex watch with the serial number 21E53170. Among the presidential staff, Zardari’s military secretary received a Rolex watch with the model number F99254CO on Jan 20, the chief security officer received an IWC wristwatch, and the ADC (Air) received an Omega wristwatch. The principal staff officer and the spokesperson for the president also received a wristwatch each. National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq received a large ceramic jar, while Senator Saleem Mandviwalla received a Bvlgari watch. NAB Chairman retired Lt Gen Nazir Ahmed received a wristwatch and an INTERPOL commemorative centenary book. Deputy Chief of State Protocol Hafeezullah received a Tag Heuer watch. Other officials receiving gifts included Special Assistant to PM on Foreign Affairs Tariq Fatemi, who received a Rolex watch with the serial number 52984286 and a hand-chased tea set on March 5. Mosharraf Ali Zaidi, the prime minister’s spokesperson on foreign media, received a Tag Heuer watch on March 9, while Special Assistant to PM on Industries and Production Haroon Akhter received a hand-chased tea set plated with 24-karat gold mixed in Uzbekistan. Published in Dawn, July 27th, 2026

items.title: Promotion du civisme: plus de 400 Etalons valident leur immersion patriotique
items.description: Le centre de formation et de production de Loumbila a abrité la cérémonie de sortie d’immersion patriotique de plusieurs centaines d’Etalons toutes disciplines confondues, le samedi 25 juillet 2026 en présence du ministre chargé des Sports. Discours, remise d’attestation, démonstration d’art martial et défilé ont été les principales articulations de la cérémonie de démobilisation des Etalons toutes disciplines confondues appelés en immersion patriotique depuis le 12 juillet 2026. Le samedi 25 juillet soit après deux semaines de formation, ils étaient en tout 430 participants dont 338 athlètes et 92 encadreurs à être présentés au ministre des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi, parents et invités. Les modules sur lesquels ils ont été instruits durant leur séjour au centre de formation et de production de Loumbila ont porté essentiellement sur l’éducation physique militaire et sportive, l’école du soldat, le secourisme, les symboles de l’Etat, l’histoire politique du Burkina Faso, la lutte contre l’extrémisme violent, la sécurité, le dopage, l’hygiène et la santé. Au sortir de cette initiation, les bénéficiaires ont dit avoir eu droit à une expérience riche en enseignements qui a renforcé leur conviction que le développement du Burkina Faso repose sur l’engagement de tous ses fils et filles et que le sport constitue un puissant levier de cohésion nationale, de rayonnement international et de promotion des idéaux de la nation. « Nous prenons l’engagement de toujours combattre toute forme de résignation, de porter haut le drapeau national et de servir notre patrie avec discipline, intégrité et loyauté. Désormais le maillot national représente pour nous plus qu’un équipement sportif. Il incarne l’honneur, la souveraineté et l’espérance de tout un peuple », a insisté leur délégué Issiaka Zangré. Un engagement salué par les formateurs qui, à travers le directeur général de l’Agence Faso Bolé, le colonel Haïdara Moctar Taboré les a invités à faire des valeurs qui leur ont été inculquées leur première source d’inspiration à chacune de leurs sorties. « Que ces valeurs nourrissent votre courage dans l’effort, votre détermination dans l’adversité et votre humilité dans la victoire », a conseillé l’officier. Le ministre en charge des sports Annick Pikbougoum/ Zingué n’en attend pas moins des immergés. Elle a indiqué que face aux défis de notre temps, notre nation a choisi de se relever par ses propres forces, de défendre sa souveraineté et de bâtir son avenir autour des valeurs de patriotisme, de discipline, de sacrifice et d’engagement citoyen. Cette marche interpelle chaque Burkinabè dans son domaine de compétence à apporter sa contribution, a-t-elle rappelé. Soulignant que le sport, facteur d’unité nationale, de cohésion sociale et de rayonnement international, occupe une place stratégique dans cette dynamique, elle a expliqué que la présente immersion voulue par le gouvernement s’inscrivait dans cette vision pour renforcer les capacités sportives des appelés mais également leur conscience citoyenne. « Cette immersion n’avait pas pour vocation de faire de vous des militaires mais de forger davantage votre caractère, de renforcer votre discipline, votre résilience, d’aiguiser votre sens du sacrifice, votre esprit d’équipe et de renforcer votre attachement aux valeurs de notre république », leur a-t-elle dit. Voro KORAHIRE

items.title: La victoire se dessine
items.description: Le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a procédé, les 24 et 25 juillet 2026, à l’évaluation des contrats d’objectifs des membres du gouvernement au titre du premier semestre de l’année en cours. L’un après l’autre, chaque ministre a présenté, chiffres et réalisations à l’appui, l’état d’exécution de la mission qui lui a été confiée par le Patrie. Au terme de cette évaluation à mi-parcours, la quasi-totalité des départements ministériels affichent des niveaux d’exécution apprécia-bles, avec un taux moyen d’exécution physique de 55,16 % pour l’ensemble des ministères au 30 juin 2026. Au-delà de cette performance, le Premier ministre a insisté sur les effets concrets de ces résultats déjà perceptibles dans la vie des populations. Mais derrière cet indicateur global se trouve un chiffre qui concentre à lui seul les espoirs de toute une Nation. En effet, selon le ministre d’Etat, ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, le général de division Célestin Simporé, le taux de reconquête du territoire national s’établit désormais à 74,53 % contre 73,56 % en décembre 2025. Ce niveau traduit les sacrifices consentis par les Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS), les Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) et l’ensemble des populations mobilisées autour de la cause nationale. Il témoigne surtout d’une dynamique qui résulte d’une stratégie méthodique de reconquête et de sécurisation progressive des zones autrefois sous emprise terroristes. La progression de la reconquête territoriale a aussi favorisé le retour de plusieurs milliers de Personnes déplacées internes (PDI) dans leurs localités depuis le début de l’année. Au 30 juin 2026, plus de 1,3 million de personnes avaient regagné 1 034 localités d’origine, contre 1,16 million de personnes retournées dans 871 localités au 31 décembre 2025. Dans le même temps, des avancées significatives ont été enregistrées dans les secteurs de l’agriculture, de la santé, de l’éducation, de la mobilisation des recettes internes ainsi que dans la réalisation d’infrastructures structurantes, illus-trant la volonté de l’Exécutif de conduire simultanément la guerre contre le terrorisme et la bataille du développement. Cette approche constitue aujourd’hui l’une des principales forces de l’action publique. La reconquête militaire ouvre progressivement la voie au retour de l’administration, des services sociaux de base, des activités économiques culturelles et de la vie communautaire. Les efforts engagés pour renforcer les capacités opérationnelles des forces combat-tantes, améliorer leurs équipements, recruter de nouveaux effectifs, mobiliser les populations autour de l’élan patriotique des populations et soutenir constam-ment les forces engagées sur le terrain produisent progressivement les résultats attendus. Cette montée en puissance se conjugue avec les grandes réformes économiques, agricoles et infrastructurelles enga-gées pour préparer durablement l’après-crise. Si cette cadence est maintenue, tout porte à croire que le Burkina Faso dispose aujourd’hui de réelles perspectives de recouvrer l’inté-gralité de son territoire national. Cet optimisme s’appuie sur une progression mesurable des opéra-tions militaires, une gouvernance davantage orientée vers les résultats et une mobilisation nationale qui ne faiblit pas malgré les épreuves. Toutefois, la victoire exigera la persévérance, l’unité nationale, la discipline collective et l’engagement constant de chaque Burkinabè pour sa patrie. Le Président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, affirme régulière-ment que le Burkina Faso possède toutes les ressources nécessaires pour bâtir son propre modèle de développement. Cette prospérité à laquelle aspirent les Burkinabè se construit progres-sivement grâce à la détermination d’un peuple résolu à écrire lui-même son destin. Pour cela, demeurons uni derrière les forces combattantes et accompa-gnons les efforts du gouvernement afin que le Burkina Faso achève sa reconquête territo-riale, consolide sa souveraineté et ouvre les portes d’un avenir de paix, de sécurité et de prospérité partagée. Par Assetou BADOH

items.title: Flash
items.description: Des enfants assis à l’avant des motos, parfois même debout dans les bras du conducteur est devenu presque banal en circulation. Et pourtant, c’est une pratique qui les expose directement aux risques de la circulation. En cas de choc, ils sont les premiers impactés, sans aucune protection. Le danger ne se limite pas seulement aux deux roues. Dans les voitures, placer un enfant à l’avant est tout aussi risqué, l’airbag passager, conçu pour protéger un adulte, se déploie avec une force telle qu’il peut blesser gravement un enfant trop petit ou mal attaché. Vent, secousses, impacts : qu’il s’agisse de moto ou d’automobile, l’avant reste la zone la plus vulnérable pour les plus jeunes. Les spécialistes rappellent qu’en dessous de 1,35 m à 1,50 m, taille généralement atteinte vers 10 à 12 ans, un enfant devrait toujours être assis à l’arrière, correctement protégé. Les autorités et associations de sécurité routière doivent maintenir la veille pour protéger les enfants, les usagers les plus fragiles, une priorité absolue pour réduire les drames sur nos routes. Aude Frederique ROUAMBA (Stagiaire)

items.title: Sénégal : Kiiraay- Les Patriotes Républicains porté sur les fonts baptismaux
items.description: Le Président sénégalais, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, a officiellement lancé, samedi 25 juillet 2026 à Dakar, son nouveau parti politique baptisé « Kiiraay- Les Patriotes Républicains. La rupture est désormais officielle entre Ousmane Sonko et le Président Bassirou Diomaye Faye. En effet, ce dernier a créé son parti politique baptisé « Kiiraay-Les Patriotes Républicains », présenté lors d’une assemblée générale constitutive, samedi 25 juillet 2026, à Dakar au Sénégal. La création de Kiiraay-Les Patriotes Républicains intervient dans un contexte de tensions persistantes entre le chef de l’Etat et son ancien allié, Ousmane Sonko, aujourd’hui Président de l’Assemblée nationale. La création de ce nouveau parti intervient au terme d’un processus de restructuration engagé, en novembre 2025 sous la supervision d’Aminata Touré, chargée par le chef de l’Etat de fédérer ses soutiens au sein d’une formation politique unifiée. Bassirou Diomaye Faye a présenté Kiiraay-Les Patriotes Républicains comme un projet politique appelé à s’inscrire dans la durée, en s’appuyant sur des valeurs de pro-ximité, de patriotisme et de rassemblement. « Aujourd’hui, nous fondons une maison commune. Fonder, c’est semer une graine », a-t-il déclaré. Evoquant son parcours personnel, le chef de l’Etat a rappelé ses origines rurales pour illustrer sa conception de l’engagement politique. Il a appelé ses partisans à pri-vilégier le travail de terrain plutôt que les polémiques. « Le temps est le plus honnête des juges. Chez nous, un paysan ne passe pas sa saison à maudire l’herbe folle… Me voici donc au champ », a lancé le président, estimant que Kiiraay constitue une « semence nouvelle » destinée à s’enraciner dans toutes les communes du Sénégal ainsi qu’au sein de la diaspora. Le lancement de cette formation politique marque un tournant dans l’organisation du camp présidentiel. A son accession à la magistrature suprême, Bassirou Diomaye Faye avait quitté le poste de secrétaire général du PASTEF, afin de respecter le principe de séparation entre la fonction présidentielle et la direction d’un parti politique. Avec la création de Kiiraay-Les Patriotes Républicains, plusieurs ministres et responsables de la majorité, jusque-là membres de différentes formations politiques, sont désormais appelés à clarifier leur appartenance en rejoignant, de manière exclusive, la nouvelle structure. Selon les responsables de la nouvelle formation, un congrès national sera organisé à la fin de l’hivernage, afin de mettre en place les instances dirigeantes du parti. Cette échéance sera précédée d’une tournée nationale destinée à mobiliser les militants dans l’ensemble des régions du pays et au sein de la diaspora. En décidant de lancer son propre parti, Bassirou Diomaye Faye franchit une nouvelle étape de son parcours politique et confirme son choix d’évoluer désormais sous une bannière distincte de celle du PASTEF. Par ailleurs, les tensions se poursuivent. L’Assemblée nationale, dirigée donc par Ousmane Sonko, a adopté fin juin un projet de loi visant à interdire au chef de l’Etat de diriger un parti politique ou une coalition de partis. Cependant, le Conseil constitutionnel a invalidé cette mesure moins de deux semaines plus tard. Ce qui a donc permis à Bassirou Diomaye Faye de bel et bien créer son parti. Soumaïla BONKOUNGOU
